contracts.title: Three row sources and the distinct candidate-relative uses result
contracts.subject: source-level obligations over supplied checked graph, interpretation, claims and candidate-signature facts
contracts.rests_on: REC-001/002/004 and ADM-001 only in their bounded checked-fact scope; no complete traversal/admission implementation is borrowed.
contracts.premise: Supply checked term/rule edges, resolved candidate-signature operations, constructor/pattern identities, selected interpretation images and the claims/evidence on which the term relies.
contracts.text:
The row has three sources.

Source(i) follows declared operations, effects and laws reachable through arguments and defined-symbol rules, less what selected interpretations replace.

Sort declarations and data constructors are not row entries.

A defined or evaluated recursive symbol without evidence that it ends contributes possible nontermination; this is not an assumption that it terminates.

Source(ii) contains claims relied on but settled never by name.

Source(iii) contributes the rows of evidence for the other relied-on claims, including builds, checking programs with assumptions and derivation laws.

Their separate provenance is retained, rather than treating a flat free-symbol projection as the whole row.

The same text also yields a separate uses result relative to a supplied candidate signature.

For that result, stop at an operation listed by that signature and report the operation as a use.

Enter every other defined symbol's rules regardless of sorts in its own signature.

A constructor of the relevant sort and a pattern matching one are uses, despite constructors being excluded from the row result.

The row result continues through defined rules; the uses stopping rule must not truncate the row.

The uses result is counted in the trusted base.

The supplied finite graph is metanotation, not a representation implementation.

contracts.title: Meaning and artefact rows, attributed entries and staged safeguards
contracts.subject: source obligations for row accounting before and after representation under supplied checked settlements
contracts.rests_on: ADM-001/003 preserve checked obligations/guard behavior; REC-004 supplements them. EV-121 is phase-specific and is not extended to every ordinary runtime test.
contracts.premise: Supply the stated term, its checked admission settlement/evidence/test obligations, candidate representation obligations, entry source/role/time and the applicable bound scope.
contracts.text:
The meaning row accounts for the term as stated from all three sources.

A membership settled by representation-independent evidence, by a test at each evaluation with possible failure in meaning, or never by name is accounted for as stated; slice1 named membership remains refused.

Later representation evidence that permits a test to be dropped belongs with that representation's trackers and tracking claims in the artefact row and does not rewrite meaning settlement.

A representation explicitly named by the stated term as membership ground is already part of its meaning.

Retain each entry's source, its does/assumes/trusts role and acting time.

Source(i) may act at run or when a bound argument is called.

Source(iii) acts at build, load, once in a run or each evaluation; only the last two act in a run.

A bound states which it limits.

A guard's reaches enter before the bound is read.

A check made only by the artefact belongs there.

Rows disclose effects, possible nontermination, choices, axioms, tools and target; they do not order execution.

Slice1 may conservatively count every entry as acting in the run, without erasing metadata or silently defining every scope.

Preserve R13's five-stage obligations, each ending with claims stored: Read text/tree/graph and turn argument effects into left-to-right continuations; retain the tree for messages and formatting only.

Mean checks membership/laws/use-once and records unresolved claims as unknown with when they could be settled; Row computes and checks meaning, whose failure is final; Represent reads licences and adds representation rows/guards before checking artefact again; Emit decodes emitted bytes with the machine theory's own decoder and compares.

Decode equality establishes the chosen machine program, tracking establishes its meaning and load checks exact bytes/bindings: one does not replace another.

A later analysis cannot rescue refused possible failure unless brought forward as evidence for the term as stated.

For rule10 machine-model guards, discharge is yes or a test at each evaluation, never a named assumption even if permitted by a bound.

Evidence dependencies have no source(ii), and their declared laws must be declared by that machine theory.

Other guards retain the source's separate allowed-assumption/semantic-lock boundary, not a new slice1 membership opt-in.

Slice1 root discloses backend, lowering and reader by name while their tracking is unevidenced, and a selected compilation discloses its target.

In slice 1 the default representation's tracking claim is settled never, and that is why the root row names the lowering and the backend.

For the generated C route, the outside C compiler's recorded output is the comparison program of D-STG-2.

For the generated C route, the independently decoded executable bytes are compared, under named bindings, with the outside C compiler's recorded output.

All checked rows and licences are premises; no stage implementation or machine-memory proof is claimed.
contracts.excludes: PROPOSED No silent meaning rewrite, deletion of test observations/costs from yes alone, machine assumption exception, concrete target/backend, selected general trust ban, completed semantics of stages or future representation/planner activation.

contracts.title: Bound substitution and symbolic settlement readings
contracts.subject: conditional row-variable, shared-polynomial, job and row-exit obligations, without a planner or full checker
contracts.rests_on: REC-002 and ADM-001/003 only as checked context/guard obligations; ADM ADG-012 retains missing bound-parameter row-variable fields.
contracts.premise: Supply checked declared row bounds/row variables, argument and evaluation rows, attributed entries, lawful-answer universe and any settlement-job costs/evidence.
contracts.text:
A bound parameter names a row variable; the declared operation bound may contain it.

Substitute the argument's row for that variable and retain everything evaluating the argument itself reaches.

A definition is checked against its declared bound.

Represent alternatives as a shared unexpanded symbolic polynomial: selected evidence/representation/tracker routes add, joint requirements multiply, its free symbols are what a reader sees and Boolean reading answers a bound.

Both branches of a runtime conditional contribute requirements; they are not two routes from which a checker may choose one.

A chosen plan retains its chosen routes.

Its cost reading bounds settlement cost only where each job has one fixed nonnegative cost and every piece of work is counted.

Places share a settlement job only with the same checking program, input, context (including evidence/route) and settled-at time.

Each evaluation of a guard is paid; different checker inputs are different jobs.

A route costs its distinct jobs at their required multiplicities.

Cheapest-route selection contains cheapest-cover search.

Runtime cost is counted on the chosen plan's executed steps, not read off the row.

A symbol leaves by answer only when an interpretation supplies it and its claims are yes, or by indifference only when every lawful answer gives the client the same observations.

Slice 1 has one fixed bound and exports no operation that takes a function.

Local fixture enumeration is verification metanotation, not stored row expansion or an installed cheapest-route algorithm.

contracts.premise: Supply the chosen output operation identity/signature/host implementation, applicable attributed-row scope, successful declaration/input/value/reply admission as appropriate, checked observations/consumption evidence and sufficient fuel under an eventual complete common schedule. Refusal/fuel-cut cases state their exceptions.
contracts.text:
Under R13 D-ROW-9, slice1 permits one output operation reached through Ask; possible nontermination is permitted; pick is refused.

The output-only choice does not remove B-07 from entry/result/failure states or compiled consumption.

No named membership opt-in is added.

All other admission/way-to-run and applicable bound obligations remain.

Compiled stops for memory are permitted only with the resource named in its applicable row/bound scope and the sourced qualified stop obligations.

At such a stop, requests form an ordered reference prefix with equal observed arguments, and each consumed value is one the reference consumes, no more often.

Record stopped, never agreement.

Prefix alone is insufficient; held-set equality is a failure requirement, not a new resource-stop requirement.

Normal agreement still requires outcome/request and separately checked value-for-value, activation-for-activation consumption; reference counts alone do not check the compiled side.

Each required literal-check run, including literal components of replies, has one fixed allowance stated with the bound, the same across hosts/runs and apart from execution fuel.

Under identical literal/checker, indices, value, admission context, evaluator state and common meter, changing the execution budget does not change that check's limit.

Finite enumerated literals and constructor admission keep distinct rules; exhausted checking leaves unknown/refusal, not a negative proof.

A reply must pass the existing instantiated-sort/context admission before resumption.

A reply that fails cannot resume; the same request/continuation remains waiting, its rejected attempt is recorded and the host may retry or end.

There is no new Loom failure.

Only one admitted reply resumes a request; an invalid attempt is not that reply.

An unanswered request remains recorded as asked/unanswered: the selected comparison policy is neither agreement nor disagreement unless a mismatch already exists, which is not erased.

Uncaught failure details are reported and observed, with held-state obligations preserved.

Equal observed arguments and use-once consumption are distinct duties.

A failed unmatched rule-bearing call reports its symbol/ordinary arguments at observed sorts, holding use-once arguments outside the payload; a declaration with no way to run is separately refused.

A run cut short by fuel shows no agreement. It shows no disagreement beyond what its completed prefix has already established: only the part not yet compared is inconclusive.

Checking a reply does not transfer ownership of what it carries.

Until the reply is committed, its use-once values remain the host's and are not added to the run's held account; refusal neither consumes nor drops them.

After the check has passed, all preparation needed to accept the reply and account for its values must succeed, and the charges required for that transition must be paid, before ownership changes.

The reply is then admitted and ownership transferred exactly once, with those values accounted for by the run before the continuation can use them.

If a required charge cannot be paid before commitment, ownership has not passed: the reply's values are still the host's, and the run's held account is as it was before the reply.

Once commitment has happened, a later stop accounts for the admitted values under D-UO-12.

A mismatch is established when no continuation of the cut run could remove it: a request in the compared prefix that differs in order, in operation or in an observed argument, or a use-once value consumed twice.

For a comparison under the matching choices and tracking claim of D-RUN-9, distinguish three conclusions.

Agreement is established only when both runs have returned or ended in corresponding failures and all requirements above have been checked: every request in order, the related outcome and held account at failure, and consumption value for value and activation for activation, with any licensed change.

An established mismatch is one checked violation of those requirements, or of the applicable stop requirements, that no continuation of the unfinished runs could remove.

One such violation suffices, even when other parts remain unexamined.

Otherwise the full comparison is incomplete, with what remains unexamined or unchecked and why.

This includes a fuel cut, a host wait, a permitted resource stop, a first-call build stop whose comparison is unfinished, and a match of requests and outcome with use not checked.

A permitted resource stop is still recorded as such; whether its prefix and consumption requirements were checked is stated separately.

Different outcomes or held accounts allowed by D-TR-17 and D-RUN-10 are not by themselves mismatches.

An incomplete comparison never establishes agreement or withdraws an established mismatch.

Where the meaning leaves a choice open, the comparison keeps D-RUN-9's requirement that the compiled run be one of the permitted reference runs.

The record of a resource stop names the resource and its cause, what the program was doing, and the artefact row entry and applicable bound that permit the stop.

It binds the stop to the run and tracking claim under which D-RUN-10's ordered prefix and consumption requirements are checked.

Naming an entry alone does not establish permission or discharge the comparison.

Where the applicable row and bound are established and do not permit the resource stop, it violates D-RUN-9.

Missing or unchecked evidence of that permission is reported as such, not treated as permission or by itself as proof of a mismatch.
contracts.case: PROPOSED S1–S12 freshly rederive every ROW1-A smallest case under the selected answers and its explicit checked-admission/observed-sort/fuel premises. S1 uses symbolic bytes68 and an admitted Unit reply; S2 retains waiting after natural7; S3 forbids a second resumption; S4/S5 produce ordinary failure payload and separate held h; S6 refuses a forbidden implemented operation; S7 is a qualified memory stop; S8 distinguishes A,B from B,A with valid local numbering; S9 stipulates the fuel cut; S10 refuses pick; S11 is admitted only under all other premises and finite ordinary-call fuel; S12 refuses a function-taking export. H1–H9 and B1–B4 check retry/wait/report/consumption, output-only limits, and fixed allowance separated from execution fuel. Tags and finite cost parameters are metanotation, not a wire format, selected allowance or complete checker/meter.
contracts.excludes: PROPOSED No new host failure/effect, actual operation/target binding, numerical allowance, free checking, automatic depth permission, replay/schema/continuation implementation, dynamic use-once proof, equal-held resource-stop rule, recovery, whole-run numeric budget or promotion of author checks into conformance.

r13_basis.quote: The exact output symbol and signature, separate depth policy, complete scope of the bound, numeric allowance and charging protocol, and the remaining host and use-once interfaces are still open.
Three passages add to a signature without yet giving it a field here: a sort's literal check (D-ADM-3), an operation's conditions (D-ADM-6), and a bound parameter's row variable (D-ROW-9).
GAP 5: how a value of a data sort crosses the evaluator's edge is to be tested.
What each is in the reference run, and which row entry it has, is not specified here and is owed (the evaluator's gap E-21).

Until it is, the promise is the narrow one: an evaluated definition that is total by its syntax, whose result check is total by its syntax and cannot refuse a result the definition can give, adds nothing to a row beyond the build.

gaps.recommendation: Carry operational constructor/literal/condition/context interface holds: REC2 expressly lacks literal-check, condition and row-variable fields; ADM3 leaves data crossing to be tested. ADM5 five-part evaluated action/outcome and narrow row promise belong to an owed evaluator/admission rule (E21), not an invented fifth row contract. No carrier or blanket condition/function exclusion selected.

diff_lines.text: -**D-ADM-2.** A term is admitted in a context, the sorts of its variables. A variable has the sort its context gives it. An application of a symbol is checked against the symbol's signature, argument by argument, by the membership claims of D-ADM-4, and has the result sort of the signature after substitution of indices. A bound argument is checked with its variables added to the context at the sorts its parameter declares, and its body must be a member of the result sort its parameter declares. A binder carries no sort of its own. A binder that is applied takes the sort of its variable from the checked argument. A binder that stands anywhere else is refused. Each rule of a defined symbol is admitted once, as a scope: its patterns are constructor terms of the parameter sorts, each variable takes its sort from the place it stands at in a pattern, and the right-hand side must be a member of the declared result sort. Each image in an interpretation is checked against the source signature carried through the map. `[C25; C6 | approved, as forced move 10, for the checking of signatures; where a binder may stand goes with the concurrency core]` D-CONC-2 adds one more place a binder may stand, a bound parameter of a constructor, if the core is taken. That answers the choice the first text put to the owner here.

That answers the choice the first text put to the owner here. The following account of where such a pattern variable may stand is for slice 1; the full concurrency core keeps the additional places permitted by D-CONC-2. A pattern variable at a bound parameter carries that parameter's profile in the rule's context: the sorts of its variables and the sort of its result, with the surrounding signature's indices instantiated. It may stand as the function of an application. Its arguments are checked in order by the membership claims of D-ADM-4, substituting each checked argument for its bound variable in the remaining sorts and in the result sort, preserving the context and avoiding capture. The application has that instantiated result sort. Or it may stand as a bound argument at a parameter whose variable sorts and result sort, brought into the same context with their bound variables aligned, agree node for node with its profile; in slice 1 a difference there is a refusal. Anywhere else it is refused. In the sentence on a binder above, anywhere else means any place but the function place of an application or a bound parameter. The use-once side is D-UO-3 and D-UO-5. `[D-UO-3, which gives slice 1 such variables; D-REC-1's Parameter line | Claude Arch, card 0110, proposed]` In slice 1 the checks of this passage, of contexts, of rules as scopes and of where a binder stands, are the elaborator's. It is not trusted (D-TB-4) and stands in the root row with the reader (D-TB-2, D-ROW-16). The memberships those checks rest on are the obligation generator's claims (D-ADM-9). `[Claude Arch's reading, card 0110 | proposed]`

-**D-ADM-3.** A literal is a member of its sort by a claim, settled by a run of the sort's literal check on the sort's indices and the value. The check is a definition in the evaluator's language that the sort's signature names. Where it is the sort's only account of its literals, it says which values they are, and it owes no claim that it is right. A sort declared finite has no check of its own: its literals are the values listed. A sort that names no check and lists no values admits no literal. A check that is meant to agree with some other account of the sort owes the claim that it does. A check that runs out of fuel leaves the membership unknown, and the literal is refused. A value of a data sort is a constructor term and never a literal. `[C25 | approved, as forced move 10]` For slice 1, a literal check run for admission has one allowance fixed with the bound, the same for every host and run, and stated apart from execution fuel. `[owner-record-2026-11-11-row1-a-all-recommended.json, ROW1-A revision 3 O1(e) | owner (recorded)]` For the same literal/checker, indices, value, admission context, evaluator state and common meter, the separately fixed allowance removes the host's chosen execution budget as this check's fuel limit. This alone does not guarantee identical whole-program or reply admission across hosts; the other admission conditions must also match. The amount and charging protocol remain unstated. Finite enumerated literals and constructor terms keep the distinct admission rules above. GAP 5: how a value of a data sort crosses the evaluator's edge is to be tested.

The label on a result is not evidence. A build that runs a definition by other code than the evaluator owes that the two agree (D-TB-6). What an evaluated symbol adds to a row is read from its whole checked action and not from its body alone. The action has five parts, each with its own outcome: the admission of the arguments; the build that runs the definition; the run of the body; the check of the result; and the bounded run of any literal check that the result check makes. A body that is total by its syntax settles only the third. A result that its check refuses, and a check that runs out of its allowance, are outcomes of the action. What each is in the reference run, and which row entry it has, is not specified here and is owed (the evaluator's gap E-21). Until it is, the promise is the narrow one: an evaluated definition that is total by its syntax, whose result check is total by its syntax and cannot refuse a result the definition can give, adds nothing to a row beyond the build. A definition that is not total by its syntax adds possible non-termination. For every other case the row entries are owed with those outcomes. `[C25, which amends the last sentence of C7 | approved, as forced move 10]`

diff_lines.text: +**D-ROW-13.** The row computer in slice 1. It takes a node, in the context its admission used where the node holds variables. From the store it reads the rules of each defined symbol the node reaches (D-ROW-2), how admission settled each membership claim of the term as stated (D-ROW-6), and the row of the evidence of each claim the term rests on (D-ROW-4). It gives the row of D-ROW-10. In slice 1 no route is chosen among, by a planner or by a reader of evidence, so the row has no sum: it is its entries, all required. Each entry keeps its source, its role and when it acts (D-ROW-8), and slice 1 may count every entry as acting in the run (D-ROW-9). No interpretation is selected in slice 1, so D-ROW-2 takes nothing away. The artefact row starts with the meaning row and adds actual artefact dependencies, operations and checks, each with source, role and acting time under D-ROW-8. Include default trackers/tracking claim, named reader/elaborator, boxing memory stops, stack as its own named resource on the same terms as memory under K-A, 10-A machine-model conditions and artefact-only guards/build/load checks. Check this completed row again as D-STG-4 requires. The root row of D-SL-1 is the artefact row of the whole program, the row at the root of its graph. What identifies an entry, and the record's form, are the record rules' to give (GAP 5). `[D-ROW-2 to D-ROW-10; D-STO-3's row "Row of a node"; D-TB-2 | Claude Arch's reading, proposed]` The walk also reads reached signatures/declarations and the whole checked action of each evaluated symbol. It retains declared operations, effects, laws and possible non-termination required by D-ROW-2, and what each retained guard test reaches before reading the bound (D-ROW-8). These are inputs of the one row text, not extra trusted texts. `[revised on card 0111: Codex L, card 0166, ruling F48: its words, in place of one sentence; Codex L, card 0166, ruling F49: its words, added | proposed]` `[revised on card 0114: Codex L, card 0170, repair R10b, exact | proposed]`

+**D-ROW-16.** The names in the root row. The reader of text is named with the hash the build records for it, and the elaborator with it, by its own hash (D-TB-2). The evaluator build that ran is an entry of the same row, by source (iii), named as each run record names it (D-ROW-4, D-RUNEV-1). The lowering and the backend are named because the default representation's tracking claim is settled never (D-ROW-5). Under the lowering stand its two steps, the checker of the low-level form and the runtime (D-PATH-8). Under the backend stand the outside C compiler, the assembler and the linker. The machine theory, with its decoder, stands as a declaration the build takes as true (D-TB-2, D-PATH-6). A name is a name with the hash of the bytes that ran and a recipe that rebuilds them to that hash, as D-TB-5 and D-TB-6 name an unverified checker. Which compiler is named waits on its choice (D-SL-1), and the bytes a hash is taken over wait on GAP 4. `[D-SL-1; D-ROW-4; D-ROW-5; D-TB-2; D-TB-5; D-TB-6 | Claude Arch's reading, proposed]` Name also the assembly-text parser, operand resolver and binary/data comparator of D-PATH-7, or the bound component whose bytes contain each. Actual unverified checking roles retain D-TB-6. Declaring the machine theory does not prove that an implementation of these checks agrees with its account. `[revised on card 0111: Codex L, card 0166, ruling F51: its words, added | proposed]`

+**D-STG-4.** The stages in slice 1. All five stages run and produce records. A run establishes what that program returned under D-RUNEV-2; it does not thereby settle every claim in that record. Text-to-graph correspondence remains as D-TB-2 states; default tracking remains settled never, with named row dependencies retained. Read writes the graph, with the build's record of D-TB-2 for the reading of the text. Mean writes the membership claims of D-ADM-9 and, scope by scope, the result of the use-once check (D-UO-1); it has no laws at interpretations, which arrive in slice 2. Row writes the meaning row and the result of checking it against the fixed bound (D-ROW-9). Represent has no planner: it is the fixed step of the plain path (D-PATH-4), in which every sort takes its default representation with every guard in place (D-PATH-1). Nothing is chosen, so no licence is read at a site; the default's own tracking claim is settled never, which is why the lowering and the backend stand in the root row by name (D-ROW-5). The row is still checked a second time. The artefact row is the meaning row joined with what only the artefact does: those named entries, the reader of text, the compiled stops for memory and for the separately named stack resource under K-A, with the C-route clean stack-stop guard still unqualified, and each check that the artefact makes and the meaning does not (D-ROW-8). Emit writes the bytes and the comparison of D-STG-2. The fields of each record are the record rules' to give. `[D-SL-0; D-SL-1; D-PATH-1; D-PATH-4; D-ROW-5; D-ROW-8 | Claude Arch's reading, proposed]` In slice 1 the lowering's two steps of D-PATH-8, the form's check, the compiling, the decoding and the comparison are all in Emit. Represent ends with the artefact row made and checked, the lowering and the backend standing in it by name; what Emit does afterwards can refuse the build and cannot add to that row. `[revised on card 0111: Codex L, card 0166, ruling F50: its words, in place of one sentence; my words, for F16, added | proposed]` `[revised on card 0114: Codex L, card 0170, repair R10c, exact | proposed]`

-**D-SL-1.** The evaluator and the store. The evaluator of D-EV-1, twice. The records of D-REC-1: terms, theories and rules with content identity. +**D-ATT-6.** The name of a use-once value. It is a pair of a scope and a count, as a sequence's is (D-SEQ-2). The scope is made from the run's start in the same way, under a fixed label of its own, so no use-once value has the name of a sequence. The count is the reference run's own: its state keeps it beside its count of activations (D-RUN-7). It begins at zero, each making takes the next count, and no count is used again. Which acts are makings is D-ATT-7's question, and waits with it. It is not the evaluator's count of sequences, which names what an evaluator program makes, so leaving a sequence out (D-RUN-6) does not move it. No operation gives a program a use-once value's name: it is seen in outcomes, records and comparisons only. A use-once value that comes in from outside keeps the name it came with; how the host names one is GAP 7's. `[D-ATT-1, by the owner's record on OQ1 A; D-SEQ-2; D-RUN-7 | Claude Arch, card 0109 | proposed]` `[revised on card 0113: one sentence added, on what waits | proposed]`

+**D-ATT-7.** Making, moving and consuming. This passage is open, and the owner's: nothing may rely on it until the owner has answered the consuming question (the owner page of card 0112). Two points are not decided. One is whether an operation defined by rules that returns a use-once value returns the value its right-hand side gave, or a new one. The other is whether putting a value in a datum moves it, or consumes it with a new value made when the datum is taken apart. The sources pull both ways: D-UO-8 reads as a new value at each result; D-UO-7, D-TH-5 and D-UO-6 read as handing on; and D-UO-11 says by name that the rule spin(h) = spin(h) never consumes h. `[Codex G, card 0223, finding F1 | open, for the owner]` What does not wait on the answer: a run makes a use-once value at each run of a constructor of a data sort declared use-once (D-UO-8), and at each run of a declared operation with no rules that returns one, which the host or a selected interpretation answers; a declared operation with no rules consumes a use-once argument when it runs; binding a value to a let's variable consumes nothing (D-ATT-5); and what a run holds at any moment, an asked run among them, is what it has made or been given and has not consumed (D-UO-12). Under it an operation defined by rules makes nothing by returning: it hands on what its right-hand side gave (D-UO-7). A run moves a value, keeping its name and consuming nothing, by binding it to a pattern variable, by passing it as an argument to an operation defined by rules, by putting it in a datum, and by handing it on as a result or in a failure. And it consumes a datum when a rule's pattern takes it apart, whose fields then pass to the pattern's variables under the names they had. For a function at a parameter of multiplicity one no event is drafted, under any answer: whether its first binding makes an obligation, and whether passing it on keeps that one, is part of the same question, with the fixtures that Codex G's rulings G224-17 to G224-20 on card 0224 name. `[D-UO-3; D-UO-7; the model of D-EVD row 4, which packs with a move and has no operation defined by rules that returns a use-once value | Claude Arch, cards 0109 and 0113 | proposed under option C-A of the owner page; it waits on the owner's answer]`

In slice 1 the relation proposed is equality of names, and it waits on D-ATT-7: equal names can be the relation only under an answer in which a rule step changes no name. Both runs begin from one start, so their scopes are equal. And the compiled run takes its counts in the reference run's order, because the plain path chooses nothing: no planner moves a term, arguments run left to right (D-RUN-2), each run that makes a value has its own corresponding run (D-RUN-6), and the bound permits no open choice (D-ROW-9). That the order is the same is not taken on trust: the watch reports each making with what made it, and a comparison begins with the two orders of making (D-RUN-11). Before a making-order comparison is marked checked, define its maker-provenance projection and the relation from lowered events to reference production occurrences. The projection must distinguish different production occurrences even when constructor, payload and final counts are equal, including repeated occurrences in a loop. Bind this relation to the compared lowering and logical activations. Include a control that exchanges two same-constructor, equal-payload productions while keeping their source destinations, together with the correct positive control. Until that projection and its actual event correspondence are checked, record the making-order comparison as unchecked. The exact fields and encoding belong to the runtime/reference-observer interface draft; constructor kind or creation ordinal alone is insufficient. A compiled run that stops for a resource has made a first part of what the reference makes, under the same names. A lowering that changes the order in which values are made owes a relation of its own, with its tracking claim; the open point of D-RUN-6, on a sequence that nothing reads, waits for that. `[D-RUN-2; D-RUN-6; D-RUN-9; D-SL-1 | Claude Arch, card 0109 | proposed]` `[revised on card 0113: marked as waiting on D-ATT-7; Codex G, card 0224, ruling G224-45: its words, added | proposed]`

It is a log that the runtime keeps of three events, each with the name of the value and the activation it happens in: made, with what made it; consumed; and, at a failure, a stop or running out of fuel, held, for each value made or given and not consumed. Each event is raised by the runtime entry that does the act, and by nothing else. Which acts are makings and consumings is D-ATT-7's question, which is the owner's, and the entries follow the answer. This rule governs a guard and the evidence that may remove it. Wherever a test at the point of use can establish a condition, the test remains until evidence resting on no assumption replaces it. For the first build, the owner chose 10-A: nine named obligations of the build remain as trust where the available checks do not establish them. They are: (1) handle liveness, resting on the ownership checker; (2) the balance of owned references, resting on that checker; (3) issuance of a handle by this run's runtime, resting on the printer and grammar checker; (4) valid output storage that is not an input's storage, resting on the grammar and ownership checkers; (5) absence of undefined behaviour in printed C, resting on the printer and grammar checker; (6) agreement of declarations with definitions, resting on the interface checker; (7) sufficient stack reservation, resting on the backend's frame report and the runtime's reservation and cleanup contracts; (8) correctness of the runtime's own unchecked code, resting on that implementation and its review and tests; and (9) correct translation of printed code to the machine program, resting on the backend's tools. The stack obligation covers the root, the next prologue, guards, enabled helpers and emergency cleanup, not merely a generated frame. A testable part of any of these obligations still requires its check: this includes the interface checks before entry and the available output-address checks. Passing such a check establishes only what it checks. A blanket claim that these nine descriptions contain no testable facts is not made. Each residual obligation stands in the artefact row as trusted (D-ROW-8), naming its condition and the bound part of the build it rests on (D-ROW-5). This does not make an unproved checker a proved or generally trusted text. It is not a yes, and is not a source (ii) assumption that a program, a bound or a lock choice may select. It removes no available guard. It leaves the row only when evidence resting on no assumption replaces it. This set remains closed: no program or build adds an obligation to it without a further owner decision. `[owner-record-2026-11-12-rule-10-a.json | owner (recorded): 10-A; the scope of testable parts and the expanded stack obligation are review clarifications]` Checked handle tickets (10-B) and freeing nothing during a run (10-C) remain unselected alternatives. This classification does not qualify the build or prove memory safety. Any other guard may be removed by an assumed claim when the bound admits it, and the assumption goes in the semantic part of the lock. The entries of a build's own runtime are also subject to this rule for conditions marked by the machine theory. At a call, such a condition must have a yes admissible under this rule, including its requirements on the evidence's row and declared laws, or be tested at that evaluation. The nine residual obligations that 10-A names above are the one closed exception: each stands in the artefact row as trusted, is neither a yes nor a test, and removes no available guard. A checker returning yes supplies no further claim by itself: D-RUNEV-2 governs its soundness claim and the scope in which a trusted text is trusted. This application gives no extra checker trusted status and creates no further exception for an untestable condition. `[Claude Arch, card 0105, on O17; narrowed by Codex C, card 0562; joined to the owner's recorded 10-A on card 0125 | proposed; under review]` `[D L278; C33 | approved, as forced move 17; its wording is still to be tested]`

+**D-ATT-4.** The core let: its record, its run and its admission. A let is a node of its own, let(e, b): an initializer e, and a body b that has one more variable, which stands for the value of e. It is a different node from the applied binder of the same text, and the two differ in the use-once check (D-ATT-5). To run it, the initializer runs first, once, in the environment of the let; then the body runs with that value bound. The initializer runs even where the body never reads the variable, and reading the variable runs nothing again (D-RUN-3). A source core let begins no activation: its body runs in the activation of the scope the let stands in. This gives no permission to replace an applied binder or erase a called rule's reference activation. A rule step or lowering that uses a let to bind obtained arguments must retain the reference activation of the replaced call and attribute its consumption there, unless a claim licenses the change (D-RUN-6, D-RUN-9). A let is admitted as an applied binder is: its variable takes the sort at which the initializer was checked, and the let has the sort of its body (D-ADM-2). It may stand wherever a term may stand. A let is how a run is named once (D-RUN-4). For an ordinary value argument admitted at a sort, a rule step may bind its obtained value with a core let, preserving reference argument order and logical call activations. This ordinary-let recipe does not cover a contextual bound argument: that argument's signature, bound-variable sorts and multiplicity must remain attached to its admitted position. Keep the contextual bound-argument form until an admission-preserving replacement is specified and checked. Nothing here admits a binder or use-once function in a let initializer or adds a sixth D-CONC-2 position. For example, `square(work(x))` becomes a let of `work(x)` whose body uses its variable twice, and `work` runs once (D-TH-5). A let is taken away, by putting its initializer where its variable stands, only as D-RUN-6 allows for the initializer (D-TH-5): never where the initializer has an effect, an open choice or a possible run without end, consumes a use-once value, or makes something new. Slice 1 has no planner, so nothing there takes a let away; a let comes from the reader of text or from a rule step. The reader makes no let for an effect: an effect's last argument is its bound continuation (D-TH-6), and text that binds the result of an effect is turned into that continuation (D-STG-1, stage 1). An effect written inside a let's initializer is read as one written inside an argument is: its continuation is the rest of the scope the let stands in, which is the rest of the initializer and then the let with its body. The reader ends no continuation at a let. So under the narrower rule that form is refused wherever what follows the effect consumes a use-once value bound outside it, as the straight form of D-UO-14 is. Ending the continuation at the end of the initializer would admit that form in slice 1, and with handlers it would change what a handler's continuation covers. It is not taken here: it is one way to make the admitting answer of the owner page on use after an output. The written form of a let and its charge are not given here. `[the owner's record on OC-01, outcome A; D-RUN-3; D-RUN-4; D-TH-5; D-ADM-2; N-A1 revision 1, section 3, for the order of the run | Claude Arch, card 0109 | proposed. Its initializer and its body belong to the scope the let stands in, and that scope's sites are counted through both. So a use-once value bound outside the let and consumed in its body has a site of the enclosing scope, and no binder consumes it from outside: `f(h) = let y = work(); use(y, h)` passes clauses (a) and (b), and the narrower rule of D-UO-14 does not refuse it. `[the owner's record on OC-01, outcome A | decided; the wording is Claude Arch's, card 0109, proposed]` Where the initializer was checked at a use-once sort, the let's variable is a use-once value of that scope and has exactly one site in the body. A value standing as the whole let body has that body position as its one site, and the let's own result has its site where the let stands. Standing as the initializer is the one site of the initializer's node, and the value passes to the variable without being consumed: binding consumes nothing under every answer to D-ATT-7's question. A machine theory marks the conditions its own model depends on, such as an index inside its array. A claim that discharges one must be yes, or be tested at each evaluation. It may not be settled never, whatever the bound admits: one false assumption there could corrupt the memory that every run record rests on. The same holds for every claim its evidence rests on: its row has no entry of source (ii). And its row holds a declared law only if the machine theory itself declares it. Any other guard may be removed by an assumed claim when the bound admits it, and the assumption goes in the semantic part of the lock. `[D L278; C33 | approved, as forced move 17; its wording is still to be tested]`

+**D-RL-12.** Rule 10, a guard on the machine model is never removed by an assumption. A machine theory marks the conditions its own model depends on, such as an index inside its array. A claim that discharges one must be yes, or be tested at each evaluation. It may not be settled never, whatever the bound admits: one false assumption there could corrupt the memory that every run record rests on. The same holds for every claim its evidence rests on: its row has no entry of source (ii). And its row holds a declared law only if the machine theory itself declares it. This rule governs a guard and the evidence that may remove it. Wherever a test at the point of use can establish a condition, the test remains until evidence resting on no assumption replaces it. For the first build, the owner chose 10-A: nine named obligations of the build remain as trust where the available checks do not establish them. They are: (1) handle liveness, resting on the ownership checker; (2) the balance of owned references, resting on that checker; (3) issuance of a handle by this run's runtime, resting on the printer and grammar checker; (4) valid output storage that is not an input's storage, resting on the grammar and ownership checkers; (5) absence of undefined behaviour in printed C, resting on the printer and grammar checker; (6) agreement of declarations with definitions, resting on the interface checker; (7) sufficient stack reservation, resting on the backend's frame report and the runtime's reservation and cleanup contracts; (8) correctness of the runtime's own unchecked code, resting on that implementation and its review and tests; and (9) correct translation of printed code to the machine program, resting on the backend's tools. The stack obligation covers the root, the next prologue, guards, enabled helpers and emergency cleanup, not merely a generated frame. A testable part of any of these obligations still requires its check: this includes the interface checks before entry and the available output-address checks. Passing such a check establishes only what it checks. A blanket claim that these nine descriptions contain no testable facts is not made. Each residual obligation stands in the artefact row as trusted (D-ROW-8), naming its condition and the bound part of the build it rests on (D-ROW-5). This does not make an unproved checker a proved or generally trusted text. It is not a yes, and is not a source (ii) assumption that a program, a bound or a lock choice may select. It removes no available guard. It leaves the row only when evidence resting on no assumption replaces it. This set remains closed: no program or build adds an obligation to it without a further owner decision. `[owner-record-2026-11-12-rule-10-a.json | owner (recorded): 10-A; the scope of testable parts and the expanded stack obligation are review clarifications]` Checked handle tickets (10-B) and freeing nothing during a run (10-C) remain unselected alternatives. This classification does not qualify the build or prove memory safety. Any other guard may be removed by an assumed claim when the bound admits it, and the assumption goes in the semantic part of the lock. The entries of a build's own runtime are also subject to this rule for conditions marked by the machine theory. At a call, such a condition must have a yes admissible under this rule, including its requirements on the evidence's row and declared laws, or be tested at that evaluation. The nine residual obligations that 10-A names above are the one closed exception: each stands in the artefact row as trusted, is neither a yes nor a test, and removes no available guard. A checker returning yes supplies no further claim by itself: D-RUNEV-2 governs its soundness claim and the scope in which a trusted text is trusted. This application gives no extra checker trusted status and creates no further exception for an untestable condition. `[Claude Arch, card 0105, on O17; narrowed by Codex C, card 0562; joined to the owner's recorded 10-A on card 0125 | proposed; under review]` `[D L278; C33 | approved, as forced move 17; its wording is still to be tested]`

+**D-SL-10.** Data declarations in slice 1. A theory may declare a sort data with its constructors, finite with its values, and use-once (D-TH-7). Value parameters may name the sort being declared, and sorts may be indexed by terms (D-TH-2). A constructor takes a parameter of a use-once sort only where its data sort is declared use-once; refusal names the field (D-TH-7). The additional question is whether slice 1 admits a constructor with a bound parameter as D-CONC-2 permits under the working core. Arch proposes refusing that form in slice 1. D-UO-14's narrower rule and the unrun D-CONC-3 census motivate the proposal; they do not adopt this slice exclusion. Carry that scope question to the owner and preserve the census and review before the relevant check, signature or admission is fixed. Until disposition, neither accepting nor refusing the form is a newly decided slice rule. `[D-TH-2; D-TH-7; D-CONC-2; D-CONC-3; D-WRK-1 | proposed scope question]` Where one sort is declared both data and finite, each value given is a constructor term of that sort, admitted as such, and the sort's values are those given and no other; a value given that is no constructor term of the sort refuses the declaration. A constructor's result sort is its data sort at index terms over the constructor's own indices and parameters. An application of the constructor is admitted as D-ADM-2 has it, with those indices put in. A pattern that names the constructor brings its indices into the rule's context as variables, and that the matched argument's sort is the constructor's result sort is a membership claim as any other (D-ADM-4): yes where the two are one node, and otherwise unknown. The combined finite/data declaration also needs a consistency account: every value the constructors can produce at admitted arguments and indices must belong to its declared finite collection. Checking only the given values is insufficient. For example, a finite collection containing only nil is inconsistent with constructors nil and cons when cons(nil) is admitted and is a distinct value. The declaration check must detect such contradictions, and constructor admission must not silently bypass the finite constraint. The exact consistency procedure, its evidence, fuel and unknown outcomes remain to be specified and reviewed; this paragraph supplies neither a completed check nor a new blanket slice exclusion. The existing attribute syntax remains, and any additional restriction on otherwise valid declarations must go to the owner. `[revised on card 0111: Codex L, card 0165, substitution 10; my words, for F19, added | proposed]` `[revised on card 0114: Codex L, card 0170, repair R08, exact | proposed]`

+**D-SL-11.** The use-once check's answer, and its agreement with the reference run. For a scope in its context the check gives accept, or a refusal that names the value, the clause and the place. It gives no count. A binder that the narrower rule refuses is refused as a form unsupported in this slice (D-PATH-4). The agreement in D-SL-1's finish line is one-way, because the narrower rule refuses right terms by its make (D-UO-14, D-UO-15). It holds when, for every generated term the check accepts and every generated input, the reference run's count shows no use-once value consumed more than once (D-UO-11); where the run returned, each value it had was consumed once or handed on; and where it failed, ran out of fuel or waits, each value not consumed is named as held, and nothing more is asked (D-UO-12). A refused term whose runs consume rightly is no disagreement. One accepted term with one run that consumes a value twice, or that returns with a value neither consumed nor handed on, is a disagreement. The generated terms include, as controls, terms whose runs do consume wrongly, each of which the check must refuse: agreement on right terms shows nothing about a check that accepts everything (D-TB-6). The refused right terms are counted. `[D-SL-1; D-UO-11; D-UO-12; D-UO-14; D-UO-15 | Claude Arch's reading, proposed]` The declared corpus includes positive controls within the narrower rule, whose expected acceptance is justified by that rule. The check must accept each positive control and refuse each negative control. Refusing every term fails this test. Report both sets and outcomes. Corpus and coverage qualification remain open. `[revised on card 0111: Codex L, card 0166, ruling F33: its words, added | proposed]`

+**D-SL-12.** Proposed generation protocol; qualification still open. Record the generator by hash and any seed (D-PR-2). Arch proposes exhaustive generation up to a stated grammar size, then sampling beyond it, and a size reaching each rule and exposing each seeded wrong subject. These are protocol proposals, not a uniquely derived size. Record every generated subject and its admission result; record admission refusals and causes separately from run comparisons. State generated, admitted, refused and compared members, including controls. For the candidate, report each comparison as agreement, established mismatch or incomplete under D-RUN-9. An established mismatch fails that candidate. Fuel cuts, host waits and permitted resource stops remain incomplete with their reasons. A match omitting use checking is not agreement. Separately test deliberately wrong lowerings: each must establish its expected mismatch. Separately test D-SL-11 source controls: negative controls must be refused and independently justified positive controls accepted. Control success is not prohibited by the candidate no-mismatch rule. Evidence covers only the named members (D-PR-3). No numeric count or size is supplied. The corpus/coverage bar, including how much incomplete work may remain, still needs qualification disposition; one agreement with no observed mismatch does not establish the finish line. `[revised on card 0111: Codex L, card 0165, substitution 12; Codex L, card 0166: the whole passage as its report gives it at line 51, for rulings F35 and F37 and in place of substitution 12 | proposed]`
